title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for smoking cessation: a pivotal multicenter double-blind randomized controlled trial
authors: Zangen A, Moshe H, Martinez D, Barnea-Ygael N, Vapnik T, Bystritsky A, et al.
population: Adult chronic smokers with DSM-5 tobacco use disorder, most with multiple prior failed quit attempts; multicenter
target: bilateral lateral prefrontal and insular cortices
protocol: Deep TMS with H4 coil; daily sessions for 3 weeks then weekly sessions for 3 weeks, each delivered after a cue-induced craving procedure; sham-controlled
summary: This multicenter, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested whether deep rTMS of the bilateral prefrontal and insular cortices helps chronic smokers quit. Participants with tobacco use disorder were randomized to active or sham deep TMS with the H4 coil, given daily for three weeks and then weekly for three more weeks, each session preceded by exposure to smoking cues. The primary outcome was the four-week continuous quit rate up to week 18, confirmed by smoking diaries and urine cotinine. In the intent-to-treat sample (N=234) the continuous quit rate was 19.4% with active versus 8.7% with sham stimulation, and among completers (N=169) it was 28.0% versus 11.7%. Active treatment also produced earlier and larger reductions in cigarette consumption and craving. The authors describe it as the first large multicenter RCT of brain stimulation in addiction medicine, and it led to the first US FDA clearance of deep TMS as an aid to smoking cessation in adults.
limitations: Absolute quit rates remained modest and many participants did not complete treatment (234 analyzed in ITT, 169 completers); the study was industry-linked to the device manufacturer (inferred).

title: Smoking cessation induced by deep repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of the prefrontal and insular cortices: a prospective, randomized controlled trial
authors: Dinur-Klein L, Dannon P, Hadar A, Rosenberg O, Roth Y, Kotler M, Zangen A
population: Adults smoking at least 20 cigarettes/day who had failed previous treatments, recruited from the general population
target: bilateral lateral prefrontal cortex and insula
protocol: Deep TMS with an H-coil; 13 daily sessions of high-frequency, low-frequency or sham stimulation, with or without prior presentation of smoking cues
summary: Building on animal and human work suggesting that stimulating the prefrontal cortex after activating cue-induced craving networks can produce lasting reductions in drug use, this trial tested deep TMS of the bilateral lateral PFC and insula for smoking cessation. Heavy smokers who had failed earlier treatments were randomized to 13 daily sessions of high-frequency, low-frequency or sham deep TMS, delivered either after smoking cues or without them. Cigarette consumption, measured by self-report and urine cotinine, was the primary outcome, with dependence and craving assessed by questionnaires. High-frequency (but not low-frequency) stimulation significantly reduced cigarette consumption and nicotine dependence. Combining high-frequency stimulation with cue exposure further enhanced the effect, giving a 44% abstinence rate at end of treatment and an estimated 33% abstinence six months later. The authors conclude that the lateral PFC and insula are implicated in nicotine addiction and that cue-primed high-frequency deep TMS is a promising treatment strategy.
limitations: Relatively small sample split across six arms, so individual cell sizes were small; the six-month abstinence figure was an estimate (inferred).

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reduces nicotine cue craving
authors: Li X, Hartwell KJ, Owens M, Lematty T, Borckardt JJ, Hanlon CA, et al.
population: Non-treatment-seeking nicotine-dependent cigarette smokers
protocol: Single session of active vs sham high-frequency rTMS on separate visits; 10 Hz, 5 s on/10 s off, 100% resting motor threshold, 3000 pulses (about 15 minutes)
summary: This sham-controlled crossover study asked whether one session of high-frequency rTMS over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reduces cue-induced craving for cigarettes. Sixteen nicotine-dependent smokers each received one session of active and one session of sham rTMS, with craving in response to smoking cues assessed before and after stimulation. Active rTMS reduced cue-induced craving compared with sham. The reduction in cue-elicited craving correlated positively with nicotine dependence severity, so heavier-dependent smokers showed larger effects. The authors noted that the effect after a single session was temporary, and they framed the result as support for further work on DLPFC stimulation for smoking.
limitations: Small sample, single-session design and only short-lived effects on craving rather than smoking behavior (inferred).

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in alcohol dependence: a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled proof-of-concept trial targeting the medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices
authors: Harel M, Perini I, Kämpe R, Alyagon U, Shalev H, Besser I, et al.
population: Recently abstinent, treatment-seeking patients with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder
target: medial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex (midline frontocortical)
protocol: Deep TMS with H7 coil; 10 Hz, 100 trains of 30 pulses per session; 15 sessions over 3 weeks plus 5 maintenance sessions over 3 months of follow-up
summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled proof-of-concept trial used deep rTMS to target midline frontocortical circuitry implicated in alcohol addiction and explored neural correlates with fMRI. Fifty-one recently abstinent patients with moderate-to-severe AUD were randomized to active or sham stimulation using the H7 coil over the medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices. Treatment comprised 15 sessions over three weeks followed by five sessions during three months of follow-up. The primary outcome was percentage of heavy drinking days by timeline follow-back, with craving, urinary ethyl glucuronide and imaging as secondary measures. Craving after treatment and heavy drinking days during follow-up were both significantly lower with active stimulation (heavy drinking days 2.9% vs 10.6%, p = .037). Active treatment was also linked to reduced resting-state connectivity between the dorsal ACC and caudate and between the medial PFC and subgenual ACC. The authors call for a full-scale confirmatory multicenter trial.
limitations: Modest sample size in a single proof-of-concept trial; the authors themselves call for confirmatory multicenter replication.

title: rTMS Reduces Craving and Alcohol Use in Patients with Alcohol Use Disorder: Results of a Randomized, Sham-Controlled Clinical Trial
authors: Belgers M, Van Eijndhoven P, Markus W, Schene AH, Schellekens A
population: Recently detoxified patients with alcohol use disorder receiving standard treatment
protocol: 10 Hz rTMS, 110% resting motor threshold, 3000 pulses/session, 10 sessions on consecutive days (30,000 pulses total); 70 mm figure-of-eight coil, Magstim Rapid2; add-on to standard treatment
summary: Because existing evidence-based treatments for AUD have only moderate efficacy, this single-blind randomized sham-controlled trial tested whether high-frequency rTMS over the right DLPFC reduces craving and drinking. Recently detoxified patients received active (n=14) or sham (n=16) rTMS on ten consecutive days in addition to usual treatment. Craving and alcohol use were tracked over 12 months of follow-up. Active rTMS showed a significant group-by-time interaction for craving and a significant group effect on alcohol use, with the clearest separation from sham around three months after treatment. These benefits had faded by the 12-month follow-up. The authors suggest rTMS may provide short-term add-on benefit in AUD.
limitations: Small sample and single-blind design; effects were not sustained at 12 months.

title: Effects of 10 add-on HF-rTMS treatment sessions on alcohol use and craving among detoxified inpatients with alcohol use disorder: a randomized sham-controlled clinical trial
authors: Hoven M, Schluter RS, Schellekens AF, van Holst RJ, Goudriaan AE
population: Treatment-seeking, detoxified inpatients with alcohol use disorder
protocol: High-frequency rTMS, 10 add-on sessions on consecutive workdays vs sham
summary: This randomized sham-controlled trial asked whether adding high-frequency rTMS over the right DLPFC to usual care reduces drinking in detoxified inpatients with AUD. Eighty patients were randomized to 10 sessions of active or sham HF-rTMS delivered on consecutive workdays. Primary outcomes were the number of abstinent days and alcohol craving over six months of follow-up. Active stimulation did not increase abstinent days over six months (about 115 days active vs 124 days sham), and craving was similar between groups. The authors conclude there was no clear evidence that 10 sessions of add-on HF-rTMS of the right DLPFC has a lasting positive effect on alcohol use or craving.
limitations: Only 10 sessions of a single protocol and target were tested, so a different dose or target may perform differently (inferred).

title: Efficacy of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in alcohol dependence: a sham-controlled study
authors: Mishra BR, Nizamie SH, Das B, Praharaj SK
population: Patients with ICD-10 alcohol dependence syndrome with CIWA-Ar scores of 10 or less
protocol: 10 Hz rTMS, 4.9 s trains, 30 s inter-train interval, 20 trains/session, 10 sessions; active:sham allocated 2:1
summary: This prospective, single-blind, sham-controlled study examined whether high-frequency rTMS of the right DLPFC reduces craving in alcohol dependence. Forty-five patients were allocated 2:1 to active (n=30) or sham (n=15) stimulation and received 10 sessions of 10 Hz rTMS. Craving was measured with the Alcohol Craving Questionnaire (ACQ-NOW) at baseline, after the final session and one month later. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significantly greater reduction in total and factor craving scores with active than sham rTMS, with a moderate treatment-by-time effect size (eta squared = 0.401). The authors conclude that right DLPFC high-frequency rTMS has significant anticraving effects in alcohol dependence.
limitations: Single-blind, non-equal allocation, modest sample and only one month of follow-up; drinking outcomes were not the primary measure (inferred).

title: Deep TMS on alcoholics: effects on cortisolemia and dopamine pathway modulation. A pilot study
authors: Ceccanti M, Inghilleri M, Attilia ML, Raccah R, Fiore M, Zangen A, Ceccanti M
journal: Canadian Journal of Physiology and Pharmacology
population: Patients with alcohol use disorder
protocol: Deep TMS with H-coil, 20 Hz, 10 sessions; active (n=9) vs sham (n=9)
summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled pilot study investigated whether deep TMS can modulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and dopamine-related markers in alcohol use disorder. Eighteen patients were assigned to active or sham deep TMS with an H-coil over the medial prefrontal cortex. Blood cortisol and prolactin served as primary markers, with craving and alcohol intake as secondary outcomes. Active stimulation significantly lowered blood cortisol and prolactin, which the authors interpreted as suggesting increased dopamine. The active group also showed reduced craving, fewer daily drinks and fewer maximum-intake days, whereas the sham group showed no significant change. The authors propose deep TMS as a potential new treatment for alcoholism.
limitations: Very small pilot sample (9 per arm) and reliance on peripheral hormonal markers as indirect indices of dopamine (inferred).

title: Deep transcranial magnetic stimulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in alcohol use disorder patients: effects on dopamine transporter availability and alcohol intake
authors: Addolorato G, Antonelli M, Cocciolillo F, Vassallo GA, Tarli C, Sestito L, et al.
population: Patients with alcohol use disorder; healthy controls for baseline SPECT comparison
protocol: Deep rTMS over the DLPFC for four weeks; real (n=5) vs sham (n=6); striatal DAT SPECT before and after
summary: This longitudinal pilot study examined whether deep rTMS of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex alters striatal dopamine transporter (DAT) availability and alcohol intake in AUD. Fourteen patients underwent baseline clinical and SPECT assessment, and 11 were randomized to real (n=5) or sham (n=6) stimulation. Clinical and SPECT evaluations were repeated after four weeks of sessions. At baseline, patients had higher striatal DAT availability than healthy controls. Real stimulation reduced DAT availability and was accompanied by decreased alcohol intake, whereas sham did not change DAT. The authors suggest deep rTMS may modulate dopaminergic terminals and could reduce drinking, but note that confirmation is needed.
limitations: Very small randomized sample (11 patients), so findings are preliminary as the authors state.

title: Medial Prefrontal Cortex Theta Burst Stimulation Improves Treatment Outcomes in Alcohol Use Disorder: A Double-Blind, Sham-Controlled Neuroimaging Study
authors: McCalley DM, Kaur N, Wolf JP, Contreras IE, Book SW, Smith JP, et al.
population: Individuals with AUD enrolled in an intensive outpatient treatment program
target: left frontal pole / medial prefrontal cortex
protocol: Continuous theta burst stimulation, 10 sessions over 10 days, 110% resting motor threshold, 3600 pulses/session, with alcohol cue provocation before and during stimulation; sham-controlled
summary: AUD is associated with heightened brain responses to alcohol cues, and earlier work suggested that medial prefrontal theta burst stimulation can dampen cue reactivity across substances. This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested continuous TBS to the left frontal pole in 50 people with AUD recruited from intensive outpatient treatment. Participants received 10 cTBS sessions with alcohol cue provocation, and brain reactivity to alcohol cues was imaged at baseline and at 1, 2 and 3 months. Eighty percent completed all sessions. Those receiving real TBS were 2.71 times more likely to remain in the study at three months and 3.09 times more likely to remain sober three months after starting treatment. Real TBS also produced greater reductions in MPFC-striatum and MPFC-insula connectivity to alcohol cues at 2 and 3 months. The authors conclude that MPFC TBS is well tolerated and reduces drinking and cue reactivity for up to three months.
limitations: Moderate sample size from a single treatment program, with follow-up limited to three months (inferred).

title: Effects of non-invasive neurostimulation on craving: a meta-analysis
authors: Jansen JM, Daams JG, Koeter MWJ, Veltman DJ, van den Brink W, Goudriaan AE
population: Studies of individuals with substance dependence or food craving receiving DLPFC rTMS or tDCS
protocol: Meta-analysis of 17 sham-controlled rTMS and tDCS studies targeting the DLPFC
summary: This meta-analysis evaluated whether non-invasive neurostimulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reduces craving for substances and food. The authors restricted inclusion to rTMS and tDCS studies and pooled 17 eligible studies comparing active with sham stimulation. Active stimulation showed a medium effect in reducing craving relative to sham (Hedges' g = 0.476, p < 0.001). No meaningful differences emerged between rTMS and tDCS, between substance types, or between left- and right-hemisphere stimulation. The authors conclude that DLPFC neurostimulation lowers craving in substance dependence.
limitations: Pooled studies were mostly small with heterogeneous protocols and craving measures, and craving is a surrogate rather than a drinking or use outcome (inferred).

title: Transcranial electrical and magnetic stimulation (tES and TMS) for addiction medicine: A consensus paper on the present state of the science and the road ahead
authors: Ekhtiari H, Tavakoli H, Addolorato G, Baeken C, Bonci A, Campanella S, et al.
population: Published tES and TMS studies in substance use disorders; international expert panel
target: various (tES and TMS targets in SUD research)
protocol: Systematic literature review and expert consensus on tES/TMS methods in SUD research
summary: Interest in non-invasive brain stimulation for substance use disorders has grown, driven by preclinical circuit neuroscience and FDA approval of NIBS for psychiatric conditions that share pathology with addiction. In this consensus paper, an international group of experts reviews the state of transcranial electrical and magnetic stimulation in SUDs. It includes a systematic literature review emphasizing the heterogeneity of methods and outcome measures across published studies. The authors propose strategies to address knowledge gaps and offer guidelines for best practices in tES/TMS SUD research. They argue that enthusiasm should be tempered by caution and that the aim is to accelerate translation of basic neuroscience into clinical neuromodulation tools for addiction medicine.
limitations: As a consensus and review paper it produces no new efficacy data, and its conclusions are limited by the heterogeneous, mostly small studies it reviewed (inferred).

title: Efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation in reducing craving in patients with alcohol use disorder: systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Kim DJ, Jeong H, Kim SY, Kim YH, Yim HW
population: RCTs of NIBS (rTMS, tDCS) versus sham in patients with alcohol use disorder
protocol: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 sham-controlled RCTs published through June 2024
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether non-invasive brain stimulation reduces craving in alcohol use disorder. The authors pooled 20 randomized sham-controlled trials identified through June 2024. NIBS significantly reduced alcohol craving severity compared with sham, with low heterogeneity across studies. Safety outcomes were comparable between active and sham groups. Benefits were particularly evident for protocols targeting the DLPFC with multiple sessions and for tDCS. Effects appeared to persist four weeks after treatment, although the authors advise caution in interpreting this. They conclude that NIBS is a promising approach for managing craving in AUD.
limitations: Craving is a surrogate outcome, and the persistence finding at four weeks is noted by the authors as requiring cautious interpretation.

title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reduces cocaine use: A pilot study
authors: Terraneo A, Leggio L, Saladini M, Ermani M, Bonci A, Gallimberti L
population: Treatment-seeking cocaine-addicted adults
protocol: rTMS to left DLPFC; 8 sessions over 29 days (one daily session for 5 days, then weekly for 3 weeks) in stage 1; control group received standard pharmacological care and was offered rTMS in the 63-day stage 2 follow-up.
summary: Motivated by animal work showing that compulsive cocaine seeking is linked to reduced prelimbic cortex activity and can be suppressed by optogenetic stimulation of that region, this pilot study tested whether rTMS of the human DLPFC reduces cocaine use. Thirty-two cocaine-addicted patients were randomly allocated to rTMS over the left DLPFC or to pharmacological standard care for 29 days, followed by a 63-day stage in which all participants could receive rTMS. The rTMS group had significantly more cocaine-free urine drug tests than controls (p=0.004) and lower craving (p=0.038). Control participants who crossed over to rTMS in the follow-up stage showed comparable improvements. The authors concluded that rTMS was safe in cocaine-addicted patients and may have a therapeutic role in reducing cocaine use via PFC stimulation.
limitations: Open-label design with an active pharmacological control rather than sham, and a small sample, so placebo and expectancy effects cannot be excluded (inferred).

title: Bilateral Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation of the Prefrontal Cortex Reduces Cocaine Intake: A Pilot Study
authors: Bolloni C, Panella R, Pedetti M, Frascella AG, Gambelunghe C, Piccoli T, et al.
population: Treatment-seeking adults with DSM-5 cocaine use disorder
protocol: Deep TMS with H1-coil (Brainsway); 10 Hz at 100% resting motor threshold; 20 trains of 50 pulses (1000 pulses/session), 15 s inter-train interval; 12 sessions, 3 per week for 4 weeks; weekly psychological support for all; active n=6, sham n=4.
summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled pilot study tested whether bilateral prefrontal rTMS reduces cocaine intake in treatment-seeking patients. Ten patients were randomised to active or sham stimulation delivered three times a week for four weeks, and cocaine intake was measured objectively by hair analysis at baseline, end of treatment, and 3 and 6 months later. The time-by-treatment interaction was not significant (F4,32=0.35; p=0.87), so active TMS did not differ from sham overall. In exploratory within-group analyses, the active group showed a significant decreasing trend in cocaine levels over time (p=0.04), with reductions from baseline to 3 and 6 months, whereas the sham group did not. The authors concluded the findings are encouraging but preliminary and require confirmation in larger studies.
limitations: Very small sample (n=10) and no significant group-by-time interaction; positive findings come only from exploratory within-group analyses.

title: A randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled study of left prefrontal cortex 15 Hz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in cocaine consumption and craving
authors: Lolli F, Salimova M, Scarpino M, Lanzo G, Cossu C, Bastianelli M, et al.
population: Adults with cocaine use disorder at a single Italian centre
protocol: 15 Hz rTMS at 100% motor threshold; 40 trains of 60 pulses (2400 pulses/session), 15 s inter-train interval, ~13 min; 15 sessions over 3 weeks (5 days on, 2 off); sham comparator; 8-week follow-up; no neuronavigation.
summary: This single-centre, randomised, sham-controlled, blinded parallel-group trial (NCT03607591) assessed 15 Hz rTMS of the left DLPFC for cocaine use disorder. Sixty-two patients were allocated 1:1 (32 active, 30 sham) and received 15 sessions over three weeks, with follow-up to eight weeks; the primary outcome was cocaine lapses on twice-weekly urine tests. Dropout was high, with only about 42-43% completing the full regimen. Ten of 30 active-group patients versus 4 of 27 sham patients tested cocaine-negative (OR 2.88, p=0.18), and time to urine negativity did not differ significantly (p=0.20). Cue-induced craving (VAS peak) was significantly reduced in the active group at the end of treatment (p<0.03), self-reported days of use declined in both groups, and impulsivity improved with active rTMS. The authors suggested rTMS could help lower cocaine craving and consumption.
limitations: Authors note a high dropout rate that left the trial underpowered, erratic urine sampling, short treatment and follow-up, and no neuronavigation.

title: High frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex for methamphetamine use disorders: A randomised clinical trial
authors: Su H, Zhong N, Gan H, Wang J, Han H, Chen T, et al.
population: Methamphetamine-dependent patients (Shanghai, China)
protocol: 10 Hz rTMS vs sham; five 8-minute sessions.
summary: This randomised clinical trial evaluated whether high-frequency rTMS over the left DLPFC reduces cue-induced craving in methamphetamine use disorder. Thirty patients were assigned to real 10 Hz rTMS or sham stimulation and received five 8-minute sessions. Real rTMS reduced cue-induced craving significantly more than sham. It also improved verbal learning, memory and social cognition, with no adverse cognitive effects observed. The authors concluded that 10 Hz rTMS of the left DLPFC may reduce methamphetamine craving without harming cognitive function.
limitations: Small sample, only five sessions and short-term outcomes; craving rather than drug use was the main outcome (inferred).

title: Targeting Withdrawal Symptoms in Men Addicted to Methamphetamine With Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Randomized Clinical Trial
authors: Liang Y, Wang L, Yuan TF
population: Men with methamphetamine addiction in rehabilitation (mean age ~33)
protocol: 10 Hz rTMS vs sham, 10-minute sessions; 5 days of treatment, 2 rest days, then 5 more days (10 sessions).
summary: This double-blind, randomised, parallel-group clinical trial tested whether rTMS of the left DLPFC alleviates methamphetamine withdrawal symptoms. Forty-eight men were randomised to real 10 Hz rTMS (n=24) or sham (n=24) for 10 sessions over 12 days. Outcomes included withdrawal symptoms, sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), depression, anxiety and cue-induced craving. The real rTMS group improved significantly on craving, sleep quality, depression and anxiety, whereas the sham group showed smaller or non-significant changes. Reductions in craving were associated with improvements in withdrawal symptoms, sleep and anxiety. The authors presented this as the first trial using non-invasive TMS to relieve drug withdrawal symptoms and associated insomnia.
limitations: Male-only sample and brief research-letter report with short follow-up; outcomes are self-rated (inferred).

title: The exploration of optimized protocol for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in the treatment of methamphetamine use disorder: A randomized sham-controlled study
authors: Chen T, Su H, Li R, Jiang H, Li X, Wu Q, et al.
population: Methamphetamine-dependent patients (China)
protocol: Four arms, 10 sessions over 2 weeks (once daily, 5 days/week): (A) iTBS left DLPFC, 900 pulses; (B) cTBS left vmPFC, 900 pulses; (C) combined iTBS DLPFC + cTBS vmPFC, 1800 pulses; (D) sham. Targets located with EEG 10-20 system.
summary: This randomised sham-controlled study sought an optimised TBS protocol for methamphetamine use disorder, comparing DLPFC excitation, vmPFC inhibition and their combination. Seventy-four methamphetamine-dependent patients were assigned to iTBS of the left DLPFC, cTBS of the left vmPFC, combined DLPFC iTBS plus vmPFC cTBS, or sham for two weeks. All three active groups reduced craving more than sham (p<0.01). The combined protocol produced the fastest response and the highest responder rate (73.7%) and also improved depression and withdrawal symptoms. Baseline depression and spatial working memory predicted treatment response. The authors concluded that protocols including vmPFC targeting may be preferable to DLPFC-only stimulation.
limitations: Authors note no neuroimaging to verify target engagement, short evaluation period, scalp-based targeting without individual anatomy, a suboptimal sham with possible unblinding, and a modest sample.

title: Deep magnetic stimulation targeting the medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices for methamphetamine use disorder: a randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled study
authors: Zhao D, Zeng N, Zhang HB, Zhang Y, Shan J, Luo H, et al.
population: Adults with methamphetamine use disorder (China)
target: medial PFC and anterior cingulate cortex (deep TMS, H7-coil)
protocol: H7-coil deep TMS (Brainsway); 10 Hz at 100% resting motor threshold; 1500 pulses/session; 15 sessions (5/week for 3 weeks); sham comparator; 23 completers (12 active, 11 sham).
summary: This randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled study tested whether deep TMS aimed at the medial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex reduces cue-induced craving in methamphetamine use disorder. Participants received 15 sessions of 10 Hz H7-coil stimulation or sham over three weeks, and EEG was used to examine neural oscillations. Craving fell significantly in the active group (p=0.008) but not in the sham group (p=0.125). Active stimulation also decreased MPFC beta oscillations (p=0.007), and the change in beta activity correlated strongly with craving reduction (r=0.913). The authors concluded that repeated MPFC/ACC stimulation reduces cue-induced craving and that MPFC beta oscillations may index the treatment effect.
limitations: Authors note a small sample and call for larger studies including women and longer follow-up.

title: 10-Hz Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation of the Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Reduces Heroin Cue Craving in Long-Term Addicts
authors: Shen Y, Cao X, Tan T, Shan C, Wang Y, Pan J, et al.
population: Male long-term heroin users aged 30-54 (5-25 years of addiction)
protocol: 10 Hz rTMS vs sham, 10-minute session followed by 4 further sessions (5 sessions total).
summary: This brief report (correspondence) examined whether high-frequency rTMS over the left DLPFC reduces cue-induced craving in long-term heroin users. Twenty male heroin-addicted participants were assigned to 10 Hz rTMS or sham stimulation for five sessions. Baseline cue-induced craving scores were similar between groups (about 60 vs 62). After treatment, craving fell to about 40 in the rTMS group (p=0.015 vs baseline) while remaining unchanged in the sham group. Stimulation was well tolerated without reported adverse effects. The authors concluded that 10 Hz left DLPFC rTMS may reduce heroin cue craving.
limitations: Very small, male-only sample, five sessions, and a short correspondence-format report without long-term or drug-use outcomes (inferred).

title: Effects of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation on Stimulant Craving in Users of Cocaine, Amphetamine, or Methamphetamine: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Ma T, Sun Y, Ku Y
population: Stimulant users in sham-controlled NIBS studies
protocol: Pooled rTMS and tDCS studies; moderator analyses of frequency and pulses per session.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis asked whether non-invasive brain stimulation reduces craving in users of cocaine, amphetamine or methamphetamine. From 2,530 screened records, 12 eligible studies contributing 16 units of analysis and 321 patients were included. Overall, stimulation produced a large reduction in craving relative to control (Hedges' g = 1.116, 95% CI 0.597-1.634). High-frequency rTMS reduced craving significantly, while low-frequency stimulation gave inconsistent results. Fewer pulses per session were associated with larger effects. The authors concluded that NIBS, especially high-frequency rTMS, is a promising approach to reducing stimulant craving.
limitations: Authors note only 12 included studies, sparse data on targets other than left DLPFC, limited follow-up data, and unresolved mechanisms.

title: State-Dependent Effects of Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex Continuous Thetaburst Stimulation on Cocaine Cue Reactivity in Chronic Cocaine Users
authors: Kearney-Ramos TE, Dowdle LT, Mithoefer OJ, Devries W, George MS, Hanlon CA
population: Cocaine-dependent adults
protocol: Real vs sham cTBS, single-blind active-sham crossover; 110% resting motor threshold; 3600 total pulses; fMRI cue reactivity before and after.
summary: Building on the Hanlon lab's earlier finding that inhibitory cTBS to the medial prefrontal cortex can lower drug-cue activity in the striatum, this study asked whether baseline striatal cue reactivity predicts response. In a single-blind, sham-controlled crossover design, 19 cocaine-dependent individuals underwent fMRI during a cocaine cue task immediately before and after real and sham mPFC cTBS (110% rMT, 3600 pulses). Independent component analysis identified a striatal network (caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens) modulated by cocaine cues. Baseline cue reactivity in this network was inversely related to the change after real versus sham cTBS (rho = -0.79, p<0.001). Participants with high baseline striatal reactivity showed significantly reduced striatal activity after real but not sham cTBS. The authors concluded that mPFC cTBS effects depend on individual baseline frontal-striatal reactivity, which matters for developing stimulation treatments for addiction.
limitations: Small sample, single-blind, and acute single-visit neural outcomes without clinical craving or use endpoints (inferred).

title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A review about its efficacy in the treatment of alcohol, tobacco and cocaine addiction
authors: Antonelli M, Fattore L, Sestito L, Di Giuda D, Diana M, Addolorato G
condition: alcohol, tobacco and cocaine use disorders
population: Clinical studies of TMS in alcohol, tobacco and cocaine use disorders
protocol: Narrative review of rTMS studies; no single protocol.
summary: This review frames substance use disorder as a chronic, relapsing condition marked by craving, loss of control, tolerance and physical dependence, for which current pharmacological options are limited. It examines repetitive TMS, a non-invasive brain stimulation technique, as a possible treatment for alcohol, tobacco and cocaine use disorders. The authors summarise clinical studies applying rTMS to each of these three disorders. Although the number of clinical studies is limited, the reviewed evidence suggests rTMS may reduce craving and substance consumption. The authors conclude that rTMS shows encouraging results and could complement pharmacotherapy and psychosocial interventions in SUD treatment.
limitations: Authors acknowledge the limited number of clinical studies; a review rather than a quantitative synthesis (inferred).

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of neuromodulation therapies for substance use disorders
authors: Mehta DD, Praecht A, Ward HB, Sanches M, Sorkhou M, Tang VM, et al.
condition: substance use disorders (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, stimulant, opioid)
population: 94 studies of rTMS, tDCS and DBS in SUDs
target: various; strongest rTMS effects with left DLPFC
protocol: Pooled rTMS, tDCS and DBS studies; moderator analyses including number of sessions and target.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated neuromodulation (rTMS, tDCS and DBS) for alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, stimulant and opioid use disorders. A literature search identified 94 studies reporting substance use outcomes. Meta-analyses showed rTMS reduced both substance use and craving with medium-to-large effects (Hedges' g > 0.5), with better results for multiple sessions and left DLPFC targeting. tDCS gave medium effects on use and craving but these were highly variable and less robust than for rTMS. DBS studies looked promising but were mostly small and uncontrolled. The authors call for trials of longer treatment, accelerated protocols and long-term outcomes with biochemical verification.
limitations: Authors note DBS evidence is mostly small and uncontrolled and tDCS effects are highly variable; heterogeneity across substances and protocols (inferred).

title: Effectiveness of Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Protocols on Drug Craving and Consumption/Relapse in Substance Use Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of 208 Clinical Trials and 36 Protocols
authors: Soleimani G, Souki A, Honari S, Baker TE, Brunoni AR, Ebrahimi M, et al.
population: 208 clinical trials of TMS and tES in SUDs
target: various (36 protocols); strongest for H4-coil deep TMS and HF rTMS of left DLPFC
protocol: Protocol-level meta-analysis of TMS and tES on craving and consumption/relapse.
summary: This preprint (posted 21 September 2025, not peer reviewed) pooled 208 clinical trials covering 36 non-invasive brain stimulation protocols to estimate effects on drug craving and consumption/relapse in SUDs. TMS showed medium effects on craving (g=0.52, 95% CI 0.29-0.75) and consumption (g=0.41, 95% CI 0.26-0.56). Transcranial electrical stimulation showed a medium effect on craving (g=0.40) and a small effect on consumption (g=0.27). Among specific protocols, high-frequency deep TMS with the H4 coil showed the strongest effects, followed by high-frequency rTMS over the left DLPFC and bilateral tDCS montages. The authors frame these protocol-level estimates as guidance for future trials.
limitations: Preprint not yet peer reviewed; the strongest single-protocol estimate rests on one study and needs replication.

title: Evidence-based guidelines on the therapeutic use of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS): An update (2014-2018)
authors: Lefaucheur JP, Aleman A, Baeken C, Benninger DH, Brunelin J, Di Lazzaro V, et al.
condition: neurological and psychiatric disorders (general rTMS indications)
population: Published sham-controlled rTMS studies up to end of 2018
protocol: Expert evidence grading (Level A definite, Level B probable, Level C possible efficacy).
summary: A group of European experts updated the 2014 evidence-based guidelines on therapeutic rTMS, reviewing literature published through 2018. Level A (definite efficacy) was assigned to high-frequency rTMS of the primary motor cortex for neuropathic pain, high-frequency rTMS of the left DLPFC for depression, and low-frequency rTMS of the contralesional motor cortex for hand motor recovery after stroke. Level B (probable efficacy) was assigned to several other protocols, including for fibromyalgia, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis spasticity, PTSD, post-stroke aphasia and depression. Substance use disorders are not among the Level A or B indications named in the abstract. The authors stress that statistically significant real-versus-sham differences do not guarantee clinically relevant benefit for each patient.
limitations: Evidence levels depend on the number and quality of available sham-controlled trials; addiction indications did not reach the abstract's Level A/B list (inferred).

title: Repetitive TMS to augment cognitive processing therapy in combat veterans of recent conflicts with PTSD: A randomized clinical trial
authors: Kozel FA, Motes MA, Didehbani N, et al.
population: Combat veterans of recent conflicts, aged 18-60, with combat-related PTSD
protocol: 1 Hz rTMS (active or sham) at 110% motor threshold, continuous for 30 min (1800 pulses per treatment), delivered just before each weekly cognitive processing therapy (CPT) session for 12-15 sessions.
summary: This trial asked whether adding rTMS to cognitive processing therapy improves outcomes over CPT with sham stimulation in veterans with combat-related PTSD. Of 515 people screened, 103 veterans were randomized to active rTMS (n = 54) or sham rTMS (n = 49), each given immediately before weekly CPT over 12-15 sessions. Stimulation was 1 Hz over the right DLPFC at 110% of motor threshold for 30 minutes. PTSD symptoms were tracked with the clinician-rated CAPS and the self-report PCL across therapy and through a 6-month follow-up. The rTMS+CPT group had greater symptom reductions on both CAPS and PCL across sessions and follow-up (one-tailed p ≤ 0.023 for CAPS and p ≤ 0.017 for PCL). The authors conclude that right prefrontal 1 Hz rTMS may augment CPT, with benefits lasting at least 6 months after treatment.
limitations: Only 60% of participants completed treatment and 57% completed the 6-month assessment. Significance was reported with one-tailed tests.

title: One hertz versus ten hertz repetitive TMS treatment of PTSD: A randomized clinical trial
authors: Kozel FA, Van Trees K, Larson V, et al.
population: Veterans aged 18-50 with PTSD
protocol: Right prefrontal 1 Hz vs 10 Hz rTMS, 2400 pulses per session for both arms, 5 days/week for 6 weeks followed by a 3-week taper, using the NeuroStar system. Follow-up at 1 and 3 months after treatment.
summary: This randomized trial compared low-frequency (1 Hz) and high-frequency (10 Hz) rTMS over the right prefrontal cortex to see which gave greater improvement in PTSD symptoms and function. Veterans aged 18-50 with PTSD were assigned to either frequency, with pulse number matched at 2400 pulses per session. Treatment ran 5 days a week for 6 weeks, then tapered over 3 weeks, and participants were followed up at 1 and 3 months. Forty-four veterans enrolled; 17 were randomized to 1 Hz and 18 to 10 Hz. Both groups improved significantly in PTSD and depression scores from baseline to the end of acute treatment, but only the 10 Hz group improved significantly in function. Neither frequency was significantly better than the other on any scale. The authors call for larger trials to test whether one frequency is better, or whether individual differences predict which frequency works best.
limitations: The sample was small and there was no sham arm, so improvement within groups cannot be attributed to stimulation (inferred). The authors note that larger samples are needed.

title: Theta-Burst Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
authors: Philip NS, Barredo J, Aiken E, et al.
population: Veterans with PTSD
protocol: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), 1800 pulses/day, 10 days of sham-controlled treatment followed by 10 unblinded sessions.
summary: This sham-controlled trial tested intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), a faster TMS protocol, in 50 veterans with PTSD. Participants received 10 days of active or sham iTBS (1800 pulses/day), followed by 10 unblinded sessions. Primary outcomes at 2 weeks were retention, PTSD symptoms (clinician- and self-rated), quality of life, social and occupational function, and depression; secondary outcomes were assessed at 1 month. Baseline resting-state fMRI from 26 participants was used to look for predictors of response. Retention was high, blinding held, and side effects matched those of standard TMS. At 2 weeks, active iTBS significantly improved social and occupational function (d = 0.39), while effects on depression (d = -0.45) and self-reported PTSD symptoms (d = -0.34) did not reach significance. At 1 month, which included unblinded-phase data, active iTBS was significantly better on clinician-rated PTSD (d = -0.74), self-rated PTSD (d = -0.63), depression (d = -0.47) and function (d = 0.93). Response was predicted by stronger connectivity within the default mode network and by anticorrelated cross-network connectivity.
limitations: The 1-month outcomes include data from the unblinded phase, and the sham-controlled phase lasted only 2 weeks. The neuroimaging subset was small (N = 26).

title: 5-Hz Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Comorbid Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Major Depression
authors: Philip NS, Ridout SJ, Albright SE, Sanchez G, Carpenter LL
condition: PTSD with comorbid major depressive disorder
population: Veterans treated at the Providence VA Medical Center Neuromodulation Clinic
protocol: 5 Hz rTMS given clinically. Patients received an average of 27 sessions (range 18-36). Self-report scales (PCL, QIDS-SR) were collected at baseline, after every 5 treatments and at endpoint.
summary: This retrospective chart review looked at the safety and outcomes of 5 Hz rTMS, a frequency between the usual low (1 Hz) and high (10 Hz) settings, in 10 veterans with comorbid PTSD and MDD. All were treated at the Providence VA Medical Center Neuromodulation Clinic. Symptom severity was measured with self-report scales before treatment, after every 5 treatments and at the end. PTSD symptoms fell significantly (p = .003, effect size 1.12, with reliable change in 8 of 10 patients), as did depressive symptoms (p = .005, effect size 1.09, with reliable change in 6 of 10). Treatment was well tolerated and there were no serious adverse events. The authors conclude that 5 Hz rTMS may be a useful option for comorbid PTSD and MDD, but controlled trials are needed.
limitations: This was a small, uncontrolled, retrospective chart review that relied on self-report measures. The authors state that larger controlled trials are needed.

title: Noninvasive brain stimulation with high-frequency and low-intensity repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation treatment for posttraumatic stress disorder
authors: Boggio PS, Rocha M, Oliveira MO, et al.
population: Adults with DSM-IV PTSD (Brazil)
protocol: 20 Hz rTMS over the right DLPFC, 20 Hz rTMS over the left DLPFC, or sham, in 10 daily sessions over 2 weeks. Follow-up at 3 months.
summary: This double-blind trial tested whether 20 Hz rTMS over the right or left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex relieves PTSD symptoms better than sham. Thirty patients with DSM-IV PTSD were randomized to right DLPFC rTMS, left DLPFC rTMS or sham, each given in 10 daily sessions over 2 weeks. Both active conditions significantly reduced PTSD symptoms, and right-sided stimulation had a larger effect than left-sided. Improvements were long-lasting and remained significant at the 3-month follow-up. The authors conclude that modulating the prefrontal cortex can ease core PTSD symptoms, and that high-frequency rTMS of the right DLPFC may be the best strategy.
limitations: The trial was small, with about 10 patients per arm (inferred). The 'low-intensity' parameters in the title are not described in the abstract.

title: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation of the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study
authors: Cohen H, Kaplan Z, Kotler M, Kouperman I, Moisa R, Grisaru N
population: Patients with PTSD (Israel)
protocol: Low-frequency (1 Hz) vs high-frequency (10 Hz) vs sham rTMS over the right DLPFC, 10 daily sessions over 2 weeks. The effective arm used 10 Hz at 80% of motor threshold.
summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled study tested rTMS over the right prefrontal cortex in PTSD. Twenty-four patients were randomized to 1 Hz rTMS, 10 Hz rTMS or sham, given in 10 daily sessions over 2 weeks. PTSD, depression and anxiety severity were rated blind before, during and after treatment. Ten daily sessions of 10 Hz rTMS at 80% of motor threshold over the right DLPFC had therapeutic effects, with marked improvement in the core symptoms of re-experiencing and avoidance and reduced anxiety. The authors conclude that 10 Hz right DLPFC rTMS has greater therapeutic effects in PTSD than 1 Hz or sham stimulation.
limitations: The sample was very small, about 8 patients per arm, and there was only a short treatment course (inferred).

title: Effectiveness of deep transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with a brief exposure procedure in post-traumatic stress disorder - a pilot study
authors: Isserles M, Shalev AY, Roth Y, et al.
population: Patients with treatment-resistant PTSD (Israel)
protocol: Deep TMS (H-coil) to the medial prefrontal cortex after brief script-driven imagery exposure. Three arms: deep TMS after traumatic script, deep TMS after non-traumatic script, or sham after traumatic script.
summary: This pilot study tested whether repeated deep TMS of the medial prefrontal cortex, given right after brief exposure to a trauma memory, could help fear extinction in treatment-resistant PTSD. Thirty patients were randomized to three groups: deep TMS after a traumatic script-driven imagery exposure, deep TMS after a non-traumatic exposure, or sham stimulation after a traumatic exposure. Patients who received real deep TMS after the traumatic script improved significantly on the intrusion component of the CAPS. Neither control group showed significant improvement. The authors conclude that combining brief script-driven exposure with deep TMS can produce therapeutic effects in PTSD, and that memory activation before stimulation may matter.
limitations: This was a small pilot with about 10 patients per arm, and the main benefit was limited to the intrusion subscale (inferred).

title: Effect of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation on Treatment-Resistant Major Depression in US Veterans: A Randomized Clinical Trial
authors: Yesavage JA, Fairchild JK, Mi Z, et al.
condition: Treatment-resistant major depression (PTSD among secondary outcomes)
population: US veterans with treatment-resistant depression at 9 VA medical centers (VA Cooperative Studies Program; NCT01191333)
protocol: 10 Hz rTMS at 120% motor threshold, 4000 pulses/session, up to 30 sessions, vs sham.
summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled trial at 9 VA medical centers (2012-2016) tested left prefrontal rTMS for treatment-resistant major depression in 164 veterans. Participants were randomized to active rTMS (n = 81; 10 Hz, 120% motor threshold, 4000 pulses/session) or sham (n = 83) for up to 30 sessions. The primary outcome was remission (HRSD ≤10). Secondary outcomes covered PTSD symptoms, depression, hopelessness, suicidality and quality of life. Treatment had no significant effect on remission (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.59-2.26, P = .67): 40.7% of the active group and 37.4% of the sham group remitted, or 39.0% overall. The authors suggest the high remission rate in both arms may reflect close clinical surveillance, careful medication monitoring and regular contact with clinic staff.
limitations: The large improvement in the sham arm limited the ability to detect a treatment effect. The population was mostly older and male (mean age 55, 80.5% men).

title: Non-invasive brain stimulation for posttraumatic stress disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Kan RLD, Zhang BBB, Zhang JJQ, Kranz GS
population: Patients with PTSD in studies of rTMS or tDCS vs sham or no intervention (2000-2020)
protocol: Systematic search of 8 databases for studies published 1 Jan 2000 to 1 Jan 2020. Random-effects meta-analysis, with meta-regression on stimulation dose and subgroup analysis by protocol.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled evidence on rTMS and tDCS for the core symptoms of PTSD. The authors searched eight databases for studies from 2000 to 2020 that compared active stimulation with sham or no intervention. Twenty studies were reviewed and 11 RCTs entered the quantitative analysis. Active stimulation reduced core PTSD symptoms with a large effect (Hedges' g = -0.975). In subgroups, both excitatory (high-frequency) and inhibitory (low-frequency) rTMS of the right DLPFC reduced symptoms, with large (g = -1.161) and medium (g = -0.680) effects respectively. The effects lasted over 2-4 weeks after stimulation (g = -0.909). The authors conclude that right DLPFC rTMS appears to reduce core PTSD symptoms.
limitations: Only 11 small RCTs were pooled, and the trials were heterogeneous in protocols and populations (inferred).

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for post-traumatic stress disorder in adults
authors: Brown R, Cherian K, Jones K, Wickham R, Gomez R, Sahlem G
population: Adults with PTSD in randomized trials of active vs sham rTMS
protocol: Cochrane systematic review of 13 RCTs (577 participants), with evidence current to January 2023. The primary analysis of PTSD severity used 3 studies (99 participants).
summary: This Cochrane review assessed the efficacy and safety of rTMS compared with sham for PTSD in adults. It included 13 randomized controlled trials with 577 participants, searched up to January 2023. Only 3 studies (99 participants) contributed to the primary analysis of PTSD severity right after treatment. Active rTMS probably makes little or no difference to PTSD severity at that point (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.27; moderate-certainty evidence), and there was significant heterogeneity between studies. Serious adverse events were rare (7 in total: 6 active, 1 sham), but the evidence on serious adverse event risk was of very low certainty. Evidence was insufficient for remission, response and longer-term outcomes. The authors call for more high-quality trials with diverse participants and standardized protocols.
limitations: Few trials could be pooled for the primary outcome, and heterogeneity was significant. Certainty of evidence was low or very low for several outcomes.

title: Effectiveness of theta burst versus high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with depression (THREE-D): a randomised non-inferiority trial
authors: Blumberger DM, Vila-Rodriguez F, Thorpe KE, et al.
population: Adults with treatment-resistant depression
target: left DLPFC (inferred; not stated in sources read)
protocol: iTBS (600 pulses, about 3 min per session) vs 10 Hz rTMS (about 37.5 min per session), 5 days/week. Up to 20 initial sessions (4 weeks), with up to 10 more if needed. Primary outcome was the 17-item HRSD.
summary: THREE-D was a randomized non-inferiority trial comparing intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) with conventional 10 Hz rTMS in adults with treatment-resistant depression. A total of 414 patients were randomized and received up to 20 sessions, with the option of 10 more. Each iTBS session delivered 600 pulses in about 3 minutes, compared with about 37.5 minutes for 10 Hz rTMS. Change on the 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression was the primary outcome. iTBS was non-inferior to 10 Hz rTMS, with similar safety, tolerability and side effects; headache was the most common adverse effect in both arms, and iTBS was rated as more painful. Because iTBS is much shorter, it could increase capacity and treatment access.
limitations: Without a sham arm, absolute efficacy rests on prior sham-controlled trials (inferred). iTBS was rated as more painful.

title: Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT): A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Cole EJ, Phillips AL, Bentzley BS, et al.
population: Adults with treatment-resistant depression
target: left DLPFC (individualized with functional connectivity MRI)
protocol: Accelerated, high-dose iTBS (Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy, formerly SAINT) vs sham, with fcMRI-guided individual targeting of the left DLPFC. Primary outcome was MADRS 4 weeks after treatment.
summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), an accelerated iTBS protocol that had shown about 90% remission in open-label studies. Twenty-nine patients with treatment-resistant depression were randomized to active (n = 14) or sham (n = 15) SNT. The left DLPFC target was individualized for each patient with functional connectivity MRI. The primary outcome was MADRS score 4 weeks after treatment. Mean MADRS scores fell by 52.5% with active SNT and by 11.1% with sham, so active treatment was superior. The authors call for further work on durability and on how SNT compares with other treatments.
limitations: The sample was small (N = 29). Long-term durability had not yet been established.

title: Prefrontal transcranial magnetic stimulation for depression in US military veterans - A naturalistic cohort study in the veterans health administration
authors: Madore MR, Kozel FA, Williams LM, et al.
condition: Major depressive disorder with comorbid PTSD
population: Veterans treated in the VA national TMS clinical program (27 VA sites, Oct 2017 to Mar 2020)
protocol: Standard clinical rTMS: 10 Hz, 120% motor threshold, 3000 pulses per session. An adequate dose was defined as 30 or more sessions.
summary: This retrospective cohort study looked at outcomes from the Veterans Health Administration's national TMS program for pharmacoresistant MDD. It included 770 veterans treated between October 2017 and March 2020, and 68.4% (n = 521) had threshold-level PTSD symptoms. Treatment used standard left DLPFC rTMS (10 Hz, 120% motor threshold, 3000 pulses per session). TMS produced large, statistically significant reductions in both MDD and PTSD symptoms (Cohen's d > 1.0, all p < .001). In the 340 veterans who received an adequate dose (at least 30 sessions), MDD response and remission rates were 41.4% and 20%. Among those with comorbid PTSD, 65.3% had a clinically meaningful reduction in PTSD symptoms and 46.1% no longer met the PTSD threshold. Side effects matched TMS's known safety profile, and the authors conclude that standard TMS is effective and safe for veterans with MDD and PTSD.
limitations: The design was retrospective and naturalistic with no control group, and many patients did not receive an adequate dose (inferred).

title: Pragmatic accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation for posttraumatic stress disorder
authors: Philip NS, Kozel FA, Walter EA, McMillan EK, Wicklund BD, Zuschlag ZD, Madore MR
condition: PTSD (with comorbid depression); MDD-only comparison group
population: Veterans with PTSD across 15 VA sites; separate MDD-without-PTSD group
protocol: Accelerated iTBS at 100% motor threshold, 1800 pulses five times a day with 50-min intersession intervals for 5 business days (45,000 pulses total).
summary: This multisite VA cohort study (a brief report) tested a pragmatic accelerated iTBS protocol for PTSD in veterans. Of 123 veterans with PTSD at 15 VA sites, 96 (78%) completed the 5-day course. A separate group of 50 patients with MDD but no PTSD was also evaluated, of whom 42 completed treatment. Stimulation targeted the left DLPFC at 100% of motor threshold with 1800-pulse iTBS sessions five times a day for 5 days. In PTSD completers, PCL-5 scores fell from 53.04 to 31.05 (p < .001, d = 1.4), with 77.1% responding and 61.5% remitting. PHQ-9 depression scores also fell, from 18.44 to 10.2 (d = 1.2). The authors conclude that the accelerated protocol produced clinically meaningful PTSD symptom reductions in 5 days, compared with about 6 weeks for conventional TMS.
limitations: The authors note that there was no control group and limited durability data (follow-up for only about 24% of patients), along with the limitations inherent to veteran cohort studies. It is unknown whether the protocol works for PTSD without comorbid depression.

title: Multimodal smoking cessation treatment combining repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, cognitive behavioral therapy, and nicotine replacement in veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder: A feasibility randomized controlled trial protocol
authors: Young JR, Polick CS, Michael AM, et al.
condition: Comorbid PTSD and tobacco use disorder
population: Veterans with PTSD and tobacco use disorder
target: right post-central gyrus region most functionally connected to the right posterior insula (individualized, MRI-guided)
protocol: Planned: active vs sham iTBS combined with cognitive behavioral therapy for smoking cessation and nicotine replacement therapy. This is a trial protocol and no outcome results were reported.
summary: This paper is the protocol for a phase II feasibility randomized controlled trial of combined treatment for tobacco use disorder in veterans with PTSD. The authors note that veterans with PTSD, about 11% of those receiving VA care, have three times the risk of developing tobacco use disorder. Fifty veterans are to be randomized to active or sham iTBS, combined with cognitive behavioral therapy and nicotine replacement. Stimulation targets an individually MRI-mapped site in the right post-central gyrus that is most functionally connected to the right posterior insula. Primary outcomes are feasibility measures (recruitment and retention). Secondary outcomes include biochemically verified smoking abstinence, craving, withdrawal and changes in functional connectivity. The protocol is relevant to the design of TMS trials for comorbid PTSD and substance use.
limitations: This is a protocol only, so no efficacy data are reported. It is a feasibility-scale trial (inferred).
